title: Linings, piping, binding and details that stay secure

say: Linings, piping, binding and details that stay secure.
This is the video for module four of Fashion Finishing and Quality Control.
A lining covers the seams, stops scratchy lace or sequins touching the skin, and helps the garment hang. Piping and binding outline and finish edges.

panel.heading: Comfort inside, distinction outside
items: Linings help a garment hang and slide on
Piping and binding outline and finish
Beads, lace and appliqué add value

say: Beads, lace and appliqué turn a plain garment into an occasion piece. But beads falling on the dance floor damage your reputation. The difference is in stabilising, securing and checking.

say: Polyester lining is smooth and affordable, but it can feel hot and sticky in Nigerian heat. Viscose or cupro breathes and drapes like silk, but costs more and can shrink, so pre-wash or steam it.

panel.heading: Match lining to garment and climate
items: Polyester: affordable, but can feel hot
Viscose or cupro: breathable, drapes well
Cotton voile: light and cool for day wear
Satin or taffeta: bridal and evening
Stretch lining: for stretch dresses

say: Cotton voile is cool for children's wear and day dresses. Satin suits bridal and evening wear. And a stretch dress needs a lining that stretches as much as the outer fabric.

say: Linings stretch less and sit inside, so they need a little extra room. Cut from the same pattern, but sew the vertical lining seams 3 to 5 mm inside the garment seam line.

panel.heading: A lining must never pull
items: Sew vertical seams slightly smaller
Hem 2 to 2.5 cm above the skirt hem
Fold 3 to 5 mm away from the zip coil
French tacks 2 to 3 cm long at the hem
panel.rule: Sew lining side seams 3 to 5 mm smaller, for extra ease.

say: Mark the lining hem about 2 to 2.5 cm above the skirt hem, so it never peeps out. At the zip, fold the lining 3 to 5 mm away from the coil and slip-stitch it, so the slider never catches it.

panel.heading: A lining must never pull
items: Sew vertical seams slightly smaller
Hem 2 to 2.5 cm above the skirt hem
Fold 3 to 5 mm away from the zip coil
French tacks 2 to 3 cm long at the hem
panel.rule: Sew lining side seams 3 to 5 mm smaller, for extra ease.

say: Hem both layers separately, and join them at the side seams with a French tack, a thread chain 2 to 3 cm long that lets the lining move.
For example, Patience in Abeokuta saw lace wrinkling over a client's hips. She resewed the lining side seams 4 mm further in, gaining about 1.6 cm round the hips, and the lace lay smooth.

say: Piping and binding are made from bias strips, cut at 45 degrees, so they bend around curves. Fold the straight cut edge down to the selvedge. The diagonal fold is the true bias.

panel.heading: Rahila pipes a kaftan neckline
items: Fold the cut edge to the selvedge: true bias
Cord 4 mm x 3.14 = about 1.3 cm round
Neckline 64 + 6 cm = 70 cm long
Clip on curves; final seam closer to cord

say: For example, Rahila in Abuja uses 4 mm cord. Its circumference is about 1.3 cm. Add two 1.5 cm seam allowances: 4.3 cm. She cuts 4.5 cm for an easy margin.

panel.heading: Rahila pipes a kaftan neckline
items: Fold the cut edge to the selvedge: true bias
Cord 4 mm x 3.14 = about 1.3 cm round
Neckline 64 + 6 cm = 70 cm long
Clip on curves; final seam closer to cord
panel.rule: Piping width = cord circumference + two seam allowances.

say: The neckline is 64 cm, plus about 6 cm for joining, so 70 cm long. She clips the piping on curves, and sews the final seam a little closer to the cord, so the first stitching is hidden.

say: Use piping to outline a seam. It shows as a raised line.

panel.heading: Outline a seam, or finish an edge
left: Needs cord and a zip foot

say: Use binding to finish an edge, such as a neckline. Double-fold binding needs about four times the finished width, so about 4 cm for a 1 cm binding. Stretch it slightly around inward curves, and join strips with a diagonal seam to avoid lumps.

panel.heading: Outline a seam, or finish an edge
left: Needs cord and a zip foot

say: Put a stabiliser behind appliqué, beading and embroidery so the base fabric does not pucker. Cover appliqué edges with a close satin stitch, about 2 to 3 mm wide.

panel.heading: Embellishment that stays on
items: Stabiliser behind every motif
Satin stitch covers appliqué edges
Backstitch every 3 or 4 beads
No long thread floats on the back
Embellish flat, before sewing seams

say: Secure the thread every 3 or 4 beads with a tiny backstitch, so if a thread breaks, only a few beads fall. Do not carry thread long distances on the back. Long floats catch and snap.

panel.heading: Embellishment that stays on
items: Stabiliser behind every motif
Satin stitch covers appliqué edges
Backstitch every 3 or 4 beads
No long thread floats on the back
Embellish flat, before sewing seams

say: Embellish pieces flat, before the seams are sewn, leaving about 2 cm clear at each seam.
Many beads and sequins cannot take a hot iron. Press them only from the back, on a thick towel with a press cloth, and tell the client how to clean the garment.

panel.rule: Press embellished areas only from the back, on a thick towel.

say: Price decorative work from a timed sample. Fatima's 60 cm neckline is 12 sections of 5 cm. At 20 minutes each, that is 240 minutes, which is 4 hours.
She values her time at about 1,500 naira an hour, so labour is 6,000 naira.
Materials are about 4,000 naira.
So the beading adds about 10,000 naira, and she explains this cost separately to the client.

To remember. Give linings extra ease, and hem them above the garment hem. Cut bias strips at 45 degrees for curves. Secure beads every 3 or 4. And price embellishment from timed samples plus materials.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Give linings extra ease
Hem linings 2 to 2.5 cm above the hem
Cut bias at 45 degrees for curves
Secure every 3 or 4 beads
Price embellishment from timed samples
